extracted.intended_audience: picture-book authors and illustrators; children's-book creators and students
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for creating and collaborating on picture books—covering character/visual design, manuscript-illustration interplay, physical format/production choices, and collaborative workflow between author and illustrator.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drawings/visuals-first genesis
rubrics_metrics.description: There were characters and a place where they lived before there were stories about them. And in that way they were drawings first.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start with visual characters and a location as the seed—develop stories from those images rather than starting with a finished plot. The interview repeatedly emphasizes that characters and place existed before text, and that this approach produces different kinds of stories (more 'concept-y' initially but with room for friendship and heart).

rubrics_metrics.name: Derive personality from visual form
rubrics_metrics.description: Try to follow their qualities personality-wise just from the fact that they are circles, squares, and triangles, and find out where that might lead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use associations implied by shape/design (e.g., triangle → mysterious/pyramidal, square → militant/squared-off) to generate character traits and story opportunities rather than inventing arbitrary personalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Localize design decisions to the story
rubrics_metrics.description: You want to base your decisions on the initial idea... follow your noses inside the thing very locally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid defaulting to a standard trim, jacket, or design; let the story/place/characters suggest trim size, layout, and other design features. Each book should be reset and designed according to its own 'suggestions and implications.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Format must match age and tone
rubrics_metrics.description: I liked the idea of it just feeling like a big block... but they got rounded off, and I think it was a good choice because it sort of also goes with how young these books feel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose physical features (board covers, rounded corners, pages, jackets or jacket-less) to suit the intended audience and tone. Consider durability (kids tear jackets), tactile feel, and how format affects perception (a jacket makes a book feel formal; jacket-less can feel mass-produced and loosen creators).

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't let design eclipse being a children's book
rubrics_metrics.description: I don’t want it to be more of a design book than a children’s book, which is what it is!
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize child experience and readability over clever design flourishes. Design choices should serve storytelling and the child's engagement, not merely aesthetic or designer-driven concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leave room in text for the illustrator
rubrics_metrics.description: If I finish a picture book manuscript and it makes sense without pictures... then I feel like I failed because it shouldn’t be a picture book.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write manuscripts that invite and require illustration—avoid treating the text as a self-sufficient short story. Deliberately leave narrative space so the illustrator can 'do some extra talking' and inform the audience visually.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write with the illustrator's 'visual universe' in mind
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if you don’t know who you’re writing for, you know the visual style and mood that is going to be there... that’s going to be doing at least half – and often more fifty percent – of the storytelling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When possible, tailor the manuscript to the illustrator’s strengths and stylistic approach; understand that physics, staging, and tone function differently across illustrators' visual universes and adapt the text accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Illustration as storytelling (not decoration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Their job isn’t just to be pretty or handsome, it’s to be a storyteller... if it has its own job to do. Informational-wise, you’ve taken an illustrator off the hook in terms of their style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design the interplay of text and image so illustrations carry plot, information, or subtext. This shifts audience focus from 'how well is it drawn?' to 'what is this illustration telling me?'

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose media/technique to support the story's implied physics and tone
rubrics_metrics.description: I used colored pencils for Sam and Dave... normally I use inks and paints that are wet, but if we used that for the dirt, it was going to look like they were digging in mud.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select materials and techniques (colored pencil, gouache, ink, crayon) to imply the right textures, mood, and physical plausibility for your story. Example: colored pencil can give a naive look that permits improbable physical actions to feel believable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use stylistic simplicity to enable suspension of disbelief
rubrics_metrics.description: I like the idea of colored pencils because it gives it sort of a naïve look... if it’s a naïve look you can get away with anything physically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simplicity in drawing and staging can expand what readers will accept (e.g., unrealistic physics), allowing more imaginative or absurd story events to feel natural within the book's logic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design sequencing and staging to teach rules/capabilities
rubrics_metrics.description: We liken it to side-scroller video games... It’s about defining this world very simply and teaching the audience what to do and what they’re physically capable of.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan page turns, staging, and pacing so readers learn characters' capabilities and the world's rules organically—use repeated visual cues and progression (like levels in a side-scroller) rather than didactic exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distill story and design to elemental ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: We talk about these stories and characters as being elemental, and we wanted to reduce everything down to the 'elements': the characters down to their elements, the story down to its elements, and then the book-making down to its elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Boil characters, plot, and design to core elements so that each component serves a clear, simple purpose. This helps maintain clarity and keeps the work accessible to children.

rubrics_metrics.name: Iterative, communicative collaboration workflow
rubrics_metrics.description: We spend a lot of time on the phone... We'd both start typing, and I’d realize, oh, Jon is still in here!... sometimes I’ll revise the text right then and send it over to Jon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use constant, iterative communication (calls, sending images/thumbnails, simultaneous revisions) and be prepared to act on sketches immediately. Thumbnails and early sketches trigger new text ideas and 'picture book magic.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose collaborators for complementary strengths
rubrics_metrics.description: You realize, very selfishly, what you’re going to get out of the other one... This isn’t going to be a good book unless we do it together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select partners whose skills fill gaps or add elements you cannot produce yourself (e.g., an illustrator who brings heart to a conceptual drawing). Be deliberate: collaboration should be mutually beneficial creatively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design characters/setting to allow series storytelling
rubrics_metrics.description: We wanted that sense that these were some stories... characters that we wanted to exist outside of these books that kids felt was a safe place ultimately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If planning a series, create characters and a place that plausibly continue beyond a single book—keep stakes manageable so characters can reappear (low-permanence world-building).

rubrics_metrics.name: Be willing to scrap and rework rather than accept compromise
rubrics_metrics.description: Both of us would be willing to scrap the whole thing before it got explosive. To just say, 'Okay, let’s go back and just try something new.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain standards for a result both collaborators like; be prepared to abandon directions that don't work and iterate rather than settle for a compromised book.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolve disagreements through discussion and mutual respect
rubrics_metrics.description: We usually default to the other’s wisdom... there’s an understanding, too, that neither of us is going to let it go until we like it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Handle differing opinions with patient conversation, willingness to test alternatives, and mutual trust—use debate as part of the creative process, not as a barrier.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider retail/display and practical production constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: This Is Not My Hat was an awkward trim size because it’s very wide, and so stores might be having a tough time with it on the shelves... Let’s make a taller book!
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for how trim sizes and shapes affect shelving, retailability, and perceived fit with other books. Practical marketplace considerations can and should influence trim and format decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid over-control—letting go can improve the book
rubrics_metrics.description: I think somehow loosens you up in a weird way... A jacket is a very formal thing on a book, so it makes it into this kind of revered piece that might intimidate someone making one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Loosen strict control (format, jacket, overly rigid text) when appropriate; reduced formality can make the creative process freer and the story less overwrought.
